title: What Counts as a Conspiracy Theory
description: Distinguishing real conspiracies from conspiracy thinking

concepts.title: Conspiracies Do Happen
concepts.contentHtml:
Real conspiracies are documented: Watergate, the Tuskegee syphilis study, the LIBOR rate-fixing scandal, the Volkswagen emissions cheat. Multiple actors coordinated in secret to do something they wanted hidden.

So 'conspiracy theory' isn't useful as a synonym for 'false'. The phrase has to mean something more specific.

concepts.title: Conspiracy Theory vs. Real Conspiracy
concepts.contentHtml:
A useful distinction: a conspiracy theory is a hypothesis that requires an implausibly large, coordinated, long-running secret to be true. The implausibility scales with how many people, agencies, and decades are needed.

Watergate involved a few dozen people and was exposed within two years. A flat-earth conspiracy would require every airline pilot, GPS engineer, and astronomer on Earth to coordinate forever — a dramatically different scale.

The bigger the alleged conspiracy, the lower its prior probability.

concepts.title: Grimes' Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
Physicist David Grimes (2016) modeled the probability of a conspiracy staying secret as a function of the number of conspirators and time. Even with extreme operational discipline, conspiracies of more than a few thousand people leak within years.

His estimates: a moon-landing hoax (~411,000 people) would have leaked within 4 years. Climate-science fraud would unravel within ~4 years. The leak probability compounds — every extra mouth is another chance.

title: Pattern Over-Fitting
description: Why the human brain sees plots that aren't there

concepts.title: Apophenia
concepts.contentHtml:
Apophenia is the tendency to perceive meaningful patterns in random data. Klaus Conrad coined it in 1958 to describe early-stage schizophrenia, but the underlying mechanism operates in everyone.

You see Jesus in toast (pareidolia), feel that recent coincidences are 'too many to be chance', or detect a hidden hand behind unrelated events. Evolutionarily, false positives ('that rustle is a tiger') were cheaper than false negatives, so we're tuned to over-detect.

concepts.title: Connecting Dots That Don't Connect
concepts.contentHtml:
Conspiracy thinking often performs a high-dimensional over-fit: it draws lines between many real data points to produce a narrative that 'explains' everything.

The catch: with enough true facts to choose from (the world contains billions of events), you can construct an apparent pattern for almost any story. The narrative isn't supported by the facts; it's supported by the sub-selection of facts that confirm it.

concepts.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Particle physicists call this the look-elsewhere effect: if you check enough places for a signal, you'll find apparent signals just from noise. A 3-sigma anomaly in one channel is unimpressive if you searched 1000 channels.

Conspiracy theorists rarely correct for this. They search a vast database of human history for coincidences — birthdays of dictators, dates of disasters, geometry of city plans — and present every hit as proof.

The math says: of course you found something. You'd find something for any story.

concepts.title: The Self-Sealing Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
A theory is unfalsifiable if no possible evidence could disprove it. Karl Popper argued that unfalsifiability marks the boundary between science and pseudoscience.

Conspiracy theories typically include a self-sealing clause: any contradicting evidence is itself part of the conspiracy. The scientist denying it is a shill. The document refuting it is a forgery. The whistleblower disagreeing is a plant.

Once a theory immunizes itself against evidence, it becomes invincible — and useless as a model of reality.

concepts.title: Inverted Skepticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Conspiracy thinking often presents itself as skeptical. But true skepticism applies symmetrically: it asks the alternative theory the same questions it asks the official one.

If 'they could fake the moon landing' is admitted as a possibility, then 'they could fake the evidence that it was faked' is equally admissible — and at that point all evidence becomes meaningless. Real skepticism demands evidence proportional to claims, not selective demolition.

concepts.title: What Would Change Your Mind?
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most useful question to ask any belief system: what evidence would convince you that this is wrong?

For science, the answer is concrete: a contrary experiment, a failed prediction, an inconsistent observation. For most conspiracy theories, the answer is either 'nothing' or 'a piece of evidence that, by the theory's own logic, would be dismissed as planted'.

If no possible world disconfirms a belief, the belief is not a model of any particular world.

title: Why Theories Spread
description: Psychology and sociology of belief in hidden plots

concepts.title: Agency Detection
concepts.contentHtml:
Humans are wired to detect intentional agency. A bad outcome with no agent (random virus, complex bureaucratic failure) feels less satisfying than a bad outcome with a villain.

Conspiracy theories restore agency. The pandemic wasn't bad luck — it was a plan. The crash wasn't a thousand small mistakes — it was sabotage. This makes the world feel more understandable, even when more frightening.

concepts.title: Esoteric Knowledge as Status
concepts.contentHtml:
Believing a hidden truth confers a sense of exclusive insight. You see what the sheep don't. This is psychologically powerful — and explains why correcting believers with mere facts often fails.

You're not arguing against a claim; you're threatening an identity. Studies (e.g., Lewandowsky et al.) consistently find that conspiracy belief correlates with feelings of powerlessness, alienation, and need for uniqueness.

concepts.title: Network Reinforcement
concepts.contentHtml:
Online communities filter members by belief. The conspiracy-theory subreddit, Telegram channel, or Discord rewards conformity to the group's narrative and punishes doubt with social cost.

This produces belief escalation: a curious newcomer is exposed to ever-more-extreme variants until the moderate version they entered with looks tame. Recommender algorithms amplify this by serving content that maximizes engagement, which often means maximizing outrage.

title: Useful Heuristics
description: Tools to evaluate any extraordinary claim

concepts.title: Hanlon's Razor
concepts.contentHtml:
Hanlon's Razor: never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by stupidity. Or, in a more useful form: by incompetence, miscommunication, ordinary self-interest, or institutional inertia.

Most large-scale failures (botched military operations, financial crises, software outages) come from systemic dysfunction, not coordinated malice. Coordination is hard; failure is easy.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor & Bayes
concepts.contentHtml:
Occam's Razor: prefer the explanation requiring fewer assumptions. In Bayesian terms, simpler hypotheses have higher prior probability and require less evidence to accept.

'A few corrupt actors fudged the data' is a much smaller assumption than 'tens of thousands of independent scientists across nations have coordinated for decades'. The smaller claim deserves your default credence.

concepts.title: Cui Bono and Track Records
concepts.contentHtml:
Two practical questions to apply to any claim:

Cui bono — who benefits? If a theory casts blame on a group the theorist already disliked, that's evidence the theory is doing identity work, not epistemic work.

Track record — has the source been reliable on previous, checkable claims? A source that was wrong about specific predictions but never updates is exhibiting the unfalsifiability pattern. Real analysts get caught and visibly recalibrate.
